os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: P1 (24 ms), P2 (3 ms) and P3 (3 ms) arrive at time 0 in that order. Under round robin with a 4 ms quantum, what is the average waiting time?
options: About 7.33 ms
About 5.67 ms
About 17 ms
About 3 ms
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: Timeline: P1 0-4, P2 4-7, P3 7-10, then P1 10-30. Waiting: P1 = 10 - 4 = 6, P2 = 4, P3 = 7, total 17, average 17/3 ≈ 5.67 ms. 17 ms is the FCFS average for this order, not RR.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: CPU-bound tasks share a core with a 1 ms quantum, and each context switch costs 0.1 ms. Roughly what fraction of CPU time goes to switching?
options: About 1%
About 50%
About 9%
About 0.1%
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: Each cycle is 1 ms of work plus 0.1 ms of switching, so overhead ≈ 0.1 / 1.1 ≈ 9%. With a 10 ms quantum it drops to about 1%, which is why quanta are much larger than switch cost (before counting cache effects).

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: Which algorithm is the preemptive version of shortest job first?
options: Shortest remaining time first
Round robin with aging
Multilevel feedback queue
Earliest deadline first
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: SRTF preempts the running job when a new arrival has a shorter remaining burst. MLFQ approximates SJF without knowing bursts, but it is not the preemptive SJF itself.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: A scheduler predicts the next CPU burst with exponential averaging, alpha = 0.5. The previous prediction was 10 ms and the actual burst was 6 ms. What is the next prediction?
options: 6 ms
10 ms
7 ms
8 ms
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: tau_next = alpha * actual + (1 - alpha) * tau = 0.5 * 6 + 0.5 * 10 = 8 ms. Using only the last burst (6 ms) corresponds to alpha = 1, which reacts to every outlier.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: Under FCFS, one long CPU-bound job runs alongside many short I/O-bound jobs. What is the classic result?
options: I/O-bound jobs queue behind the CPU hog, so devices sit idle and utilisation drops
The I/O-bound jobs starve forever because FCFS never runs them
The CPU-bound job is starved because I/O jobs keep re-queuing
Throughput rises because the CPU is always busy with the long job
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: This is the convoy effect: short jobs pile up behind the long burst, then devices idle while they wait. They are delayed, not starved forever, because FCFS eventually serves every job.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: Why does MLFQ periodically boost every job back to the top queue?
options: To reset vruntime so CFS stays fair
To stop long jobs starving and let jobs that turned interactive rise again
To make the time quantum shorter for CPU-bound jobs
To flush the TLB so jobs start with a clean cache
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: Without a boost, a stream of interactive jobs can starve long jobs at the bottom, and a job whose behaviour changes stays demoted. vruntime is a CFS concept and plays no part in MLFQ.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: On Linux CFS, two CPU-bound tasks share one core: one at nice 0 (weight 1024), one at nice 5 (weight 335). Roughly how is the CPU split?
options: About 50% / 50%
About 55% / 45%
About 75% / 25%
About 95% / 5%
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: Share is weight / total weight: 1024 / (1024 + 335) ≈ 75%. Each nice step changes weight by about 1.25x, so five steps is about 3x, not an even split or near-total starvation.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: A Node service in a container with cgroup v2 cpu.max = '50000 100000' shows ~50 ms p99 spikes while average CPU use looks low. What is the most likely cause?
options: Bursts use up the 50 ms quota early in each 100 ms period and the cgroup is throttled
The nice value of the container is too low, so CFS preempts it too often
Round robin quanta inside the container are set to 50 ms
The kernel swaps the process out whenever average CPU is low
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: cpu.max grants 50 ms of CPU per 100 ms period across all threads. A burst (event loop plus GC and libuv threads) can spend it in a few ms, then everything waits until the next period. Averages hide this; check nr_throttled in cpu.stat.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: Which definition of turnaround time is correct?
options: Time from arrival until first run
Time spent waiting in the ready queue
Total CPU time the job consumes
Time from arrival until completion
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: Turnaround = completion - arrival. Arrival until first run is response time, which round robin improves; ready-queue time is waiting time.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: The Mars Pathfinder lander kept resetting because a high-priority task blocked on a mutex held by a low-priority task while a medium task ran. What was the fix?
options: Lowering the priority of the medium task permanently
Enabling priority inheritance on that mutex
Switching the scheduler to round robin
Replacing the mutex with a spinlock
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: That was priority inversion, fixed by turning on priority inheritance so the lock holder temporarily runs at the waiter's priority. A spinlock would make it worse because the high task would burn CPU while the holder cannot run.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: Which statements about Linux real-time scheduling classes are correct? Select all that apply.
options: A SCHED_FIFO task runs until it blocks, yields, or a higher-priority RT task preempts it
SCHED_FIFO tasks are preempted once their vruntime exceeds the minimum
SCHED_RR adds a time slice among RT tasks of the same priority
Without RT throttling, a runaway SCHED_FIFO loop can starve normal tasks
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: FIFO has no time slice, RR rotates equal-priority RT tasks, and a spinning FIFO task can starve CFS tasks, which is why sched_rt_runtime_us reserves time for them. vruntime belongs to CFS, not the RT classes.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: Which costs make a context switch more expensive than just saving and restoring registers? Select all that apply.
options: Copying the process heap out to swap
TLB entries lost when switching address spaces
Cold CPU caches for the incoming task
Kernel entry and scheduler bookkeeping
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: Switching address spaces loses TLB entries (unless PCID/ASIDs are used), the new task finds cold caches, and the kernel path costs cycles. Nothing gets written to swap on a switch; swapping is a memory-pressure decision.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: Which policies can starve a job indefinitely? Select all that apply.
options: Shortest job first with a steady stream of short jobs
Round robin
Strict priority without aging
First come, first served with finite jobs
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: SJF and strict priority keep picking newcomers ahead of a long or low-priority job. RR serves every ready job each round, and FCFS eventually reaches every finite job, even if it waits a long time.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: A latency-sensitive API shares a Linux host with batch jobs. Which changes help its tail latency? Select all that apply.
options: Pin it to dedicated cores with a cpuset
Give it a higher cgroup cpu.weight than the batch group
Give it a very small cpu.max quota
Run the batch jobs at a higher nice value
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: Dedicated cores, more weight, and nicer batch jobs all give the API more CPU when it needs it. A tight cpu.max quota does the opposite: it throttles the API during bursts.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: Round robin with a quantum longer than every job's burst behaves exactly like FCFS.
options: True
False
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: If no job ever uses up its quantum, nothing is preempted, so jobs run to completion in arrival order, which is FCFS. That is why a huge quantum loses RR's response-time benefit.

os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.prompt: In CFS, a task with a higher nice value accumulates vruntime more slowly than a nice-0 task for the same real CPU time.
options: True
False
os:cpu-scheduling-tradeoffs.explanation: A higher nice value means a lower weight, and vruntime grows in inverse proportion to weight, so it grows faster. The task is picked less often and ends up with a smaller share.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: You have 16 cores and tasks that wait 90 ms on I/O for every 10 ms of CPU. Using N = cores * (1 + wait / compute), what pool size do you start with?
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: N = 16 * (1 + 90/10) = 16 * 10 = 160. 16 is the CPU-bound answer, which leaves cores idle while threads wait on I/O. Treat 160 as a starting point and tune it against downstream limits.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: A service gets 400 requests per second and each request holds a pool thread for 50 ms. By Little's law, how many threads are busy on average?
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: L = lambda * W = 400/s * 0.05 s = 20 concurrent threads. Size above that for bursts and variance; 2000 comes from multiplying by milliseconds instead of seconds.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: A Java ThreadPoolExecutor has corePoolSize 4, maximumPoolSize 16 and an ArrayBlockingQueue of capacity 100. When does it create the fifth thread?
options: As soon as four tasks are running
When a task has waited longer than keepAliveTime
Only when 100 tasks are queued and another arrives
When CPU usage passes 80%
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: ThreadPoolExecutor fills core threads, then the queue, and only grows toward maximumPoolSize once the queue rejects an offer. Many people expect it to grow before queueing, which is why it seems to stay at 4 threads under moderate load.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: A pool of 50 worker threads calls a database through a connection pool of 10. Under load, latency climbs and 40 workers sit blocked. What is the right fix?
options: Raise the worker pool to 200 so more requests proceed
Size workers to the downstream limit and shed or queue the rest
Make the connection pool unbounded
Switch the workers to busy-waiting for connections
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: Only 10 queries can run at a time, so the extra workers just hold memory and queue inside the pool. More threads add contention without throughput. Match concurrency to the bottleneck and reject or queue work explicitly.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: What is the default size of libuv's thread pool in Node.js?
options: The number of CPU cores
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE defaults to 4 whatever the core count, which is why a few slow fs or dns.lookup calls can block the rest. Set it before the pool is first used.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: What is the correct order for shutting down an executor gracefully?
options: Interrupt all workers, then stop accepting tasks, then drain the queue
Stop accepting tasks, await termination with a timeout, then force-cancel and log leftovers
Kill the process; queued tasks are retried on restart anyway
Clear the queue first so workers finish faster, then stop accepting tasks
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: In Java that is shutdown(), awaitTermination(timeout), then shutdownNow() for stragglers. Interrupting first throws away in-flight work, and clearing the queue silently drops accepted tasks.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: A task submitted with Java's ExecutorService.submit() throws a RuntimeException and nobody ever calls get() on its Future. What happens?
options: The worker thread dies and the uncaught exception handler logs it
The exception is stored in the Future and is effectively lost; the worker keeps running
The executor shuts down
The exception propagates to the thread that called submit()
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: submit() wraps the task, so the exception is captured and only rethrown as an ExecutionException from get(). With execute(), the exception reaches the thread's uncaught handler and the pool replaces the worker. Silently swallowed errors are a common pool bug.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: A slow payment API ties up every thread in your shared pool, so unrelated catalog requests start timing out. Which pattern addresses this?
options: Increase the shared pool's queue size
Use a bulkhead: a separate, bounded pool per downstream dependency
Retry catalog requests more aggressively
Use an unbounded cached thread pool
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: Separate pools contain the damage to payment calls, at the cost of some idle capacity in each. A bigger queue or unbounded pool just converts the stall into more latency or memory use.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: What is the main reason to use a thread pool instead of creating a new thread for every task?
options: Pooled threads run code faster than new threads
To reuse threads, avoiding creation costs and capping concurrency
Pools remove the need for synchronisation between tasks
The OS only allows threads to be created at startup
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: Creating threads costs syscalls, stack memory and scheduler work, and unbounded creation can exhaust memory. Once running, a pooled thread is no faster, and tasks still need synchronisation for shared state.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: In Java 21, what is a well-known pitfall of virtual threads?
options: They cannot perform blocking I/O
Blocking inside a synchronized block pins the carrier thread
Each one reserves a full 1 MiB OS stack
They can only run on a single carrier thread
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: Virtual threads unmount from their carrier on blocking I/O, except while pinned, for example inside synchronized in Java 21. Pinned threads can exhaust the small carrier pool. Blocking I/O is exactly what they are designed for.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: Which metrics help you detect that a thread pool is saturated? Select all that apply.
options: Current queue depth
Time tasks spend waiting in the queue
The configured corePoolSize value
Count of rejected tasks
Number of classes loaded by the JVM
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: Queue depth, queue wait time and rejections show demand exceeding capacity. corePoolSize is static configuration, and class-loading counts tell you nothing about pool load.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: Which statements about a work-stealing pool such as Java's ForkJoinPool are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Each worker keeps its own deque of tasks
It guarantees global FIFO order of all submitted tasks
Idle workers steal from the opposite end of other workers' deques
It reduces contention compared with one shared queue
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: Owners push and pop at one end (LIFO, cache-friendly) while thieves take from the other end, so they rarely collide. That design gives up any global ordering guarantee.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: Which work belongs in a Node worker_threads pool rather than on the main event loop? Select all that apply.
options: Resizing images in pure JavaScript
Awaiting an HTTP response from another service
Hashing large payloads with a pure-JS algorithm
Reading from a TCP socket
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: CPU-bound JavaScript blocks the event loop, so move it to workers. Waiting on HTTP or socket reads is non-blocking I/O handled by the loop, and moving it to a worker adds overhead for nothing.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: Your pool's tasks mostly wait on a database. Throughput stopped improving after you raised the pool from 32 to 128 threads. What are likely explanations? Select all that apply.
options: The database connection pool caps concurrent queries
The database itself is saturated on CPU, locks or disk
More threads always help I/O-bound work, so it must be a measurement error
Extra threads add context switching and memory without adding work done
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: The bottleneck has moved downstream: connections, DB capacity, or contention. Adding threads beyond that point only adds overhead. The idea that more threads always help I/O work is exactly the misconception here.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: Increasing a thread pool's size always increases throughput for I/O-bound work.
options: True
False
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: It helps only until a downstream resource (connections, DB, remote rate limits) or CPU saturates. Past that point you add memory, switching and contention with no gain.

os:thread-pool-design.prompt: With Java's ThreadPoolExecutor and the default AbortPolicy, a rejected execute() call throws RejectedExecutionException.
options: True
False
os:thread-pool-design.explanation: AbortPolicy is the default handler and throws when both the queue and the max threads are full. Callers must handle it, or you pick CallerRuns, Discard or DiscardOldest instead.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: In the semaphore bounded buffer, which producer sequence is correct?
options: lock(mutex); wait(empty); insert; signal(full); unlock(mutex)
wait(empty); lock(mutex); insert; unlock(mutex); signal(full)
wait(full); lock(mutex); insert; unlock(mutex); signal(empty)
lock(mutex); insert; unlock(mutex); wait(empty); signal(full)
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: Wait for a free slot before taking the mutex, insert, release, then announce a full slot. Taking the mutex first can deadlock when the buffer is full, because consumers then cannot get in to free a slot.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: A producer makes 1,000 items/s and a consumer takes 800 items/s. Starting empty, roughly how long until a 10,000-slot buffer fills?
options: It never fills
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: The buffer grows at 1000 - 800 = 200 items/s, so 10,000 / 200 = 50 s. 10 s ignores the consumer. Once full, backpressure holds the producer to 800/s, so a buffer only absorbs bursts, never a sustained rate mismatch.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: A consumer checks count == 0 without holding the lock, then calls wait. Meanwhile a producer inserts and signals in between. What happens?
options: The consumer sees the item on its next loop iteration
The signal is lost and the consumer may sleep forever
The producer blocks until the consumer is waiting
The condition variable queues the signal for later
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: Condition variables have no memory: a signal with no waiter is dropped. Checking the predicate and waiting must be atomic with respect to the producer, which is why wait(cond, mutex) is called while holding the mutex.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: With pthreads and exactly one consumer, why is `if (count == 0) wait(...)` still wrong where `while` is right?
options: POSIX allows spurious wakeups, so wait can return while the buffer is still empty
Using if causes a deadlock on the mutex
if prevents the producer from ever signalling
Only Hoare monitors allow while loops
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: pthread_cond_wait may return without a signal, and under Mesa semantics the state can change before you reacquire the lock. Either way the predicate must be rechecked. A single consumer removes the stealing case but not spurious wakeups.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: Four consumer threads shut down when they read a poison-pill item. How many pills should the single producer enqueue after its last real item?
options: One
Four
Five
As many as the buffer capacity
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: Each consumer exits after taking one pill, so you need one per consumer. With a single pill, three consumers block forever on an empty buffer.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: A bounded queue with many producers and consumers adds close(). What must close() do so blocked consumers exit cleanly?
options: Set closed = true without the lock, since it is a single boolean
Set closed under the mutex and broadcast on notEmpty (and notFull)
Signal notEmpty once; consumers wake each other in turn
Destroy the condition variables so waits return an error
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: Waiters must see the flag under the same lock as the predicate, and every blocked thread needs waking, so broadcast. Consumers drain what is left, then return 'closed' when the buffer is empty. A single signal can leave the others asleep.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: In Go, what happens when you send on a channel created with make(chan int, 10) that already holds 10 unreceived values?
options: The oldest value is overwritten
The send blocks until a receiver takes a value
The send panics
The channel grows to 20
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: A buffered channel is a bounded buffer: sends block when it is full and receives block when it is empty. Only sending on a closed channel panics.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: In Node, writable.write(chunk) returned false. What should the producer do?
options: Retry the same chunk in a tight loop until it returns true
Treat the chunk as dropped and send it again
Stop writing and resume when the 'drain' event fires
Call end() because the stream has failed
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: false means the internal buffer passed highWaterMark. The chunk was accepted, but you should pause until 'drain'. Ignoring it makes memory grow without bound; pipe() and pipeline() handle this for you.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: Producers and consumers share one condition variable and use signal, not broadcast. What can go wrong?
options: A producer's signal wakes another producer, so no consumer runs and all threads can end up waiting
Two consumers can remove the same item
The mutex becomes unlockable
Signals are queued and delivered twice
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: With one CV, a signal may reach a thread of the wrong kind. It rechecks, waits again, and the wakeup is wasted, which can leave everyone asleep. Either broadcast (thundering herd) or use separate notFull and notEmpty CVs.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: Why can a single-producer single-consumer ring buffer be implemented without locks?
options: Each index has exactly one writer, so acquire/release ordering on head and tail is enough
CPUs execute single-producer code atomically
Ring buffers never fill up
The consumer can spin on a mutex instead
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: The producer alone writes tail and the consumer alone writes head. Publishing with release and reading with acquire ensures the slot data is visible before the index moves. With multiple producers you need CAS or a lock.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: A ring buffer of capacity 8 stores its next write position at index 7. Where does the write after that one go?
options: Index 8
Index 0
Index 1
The buffer must be resized
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: Positions wrap: (7 + 1) % 8 = 0. Full versus empty is tracked separately with a count or by sacrificing one slot.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: Which mistakes in a semaphore bounded buffer cause a deadlock or permanently stuck threads? Select all that apply.
options: Producer takes the mutex before wait(empty)
Producer signals full while still holding the mutex
Producer forgets signal(full) after inserting
Consumer rechecks its predicate in a while loop
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: Locking before waiting blocks consumers out of a full buffer, and a missing signal(full) leaves consumers waiting on items that exist. Signalling while holding the mutex is legal (at worst the woken thread briefly waits for the lock), and while loops are correct.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: What does a bounded buffer give you that an unbounded queue does not? Select all that apply.
options: Backpressure that slows producers when consumers fall behind
Bounded memory use
A cap on queueing delay for accepted items
Durability of queued items across a crash
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: Capacity limits memory and how long an item can sit behind others, and blocking producers is backpressure. Neither kind of in-memory buffer survives a crash; that needs a persistent log such as Kafka.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: Which of these are instances of the producer-consumer pattern with a bounded buffer? Select all that apply.
options: A Unix pipe like `gzip < big.log | wc -c`
A pure function returning a value to its caller
A Java ArrayBlockingQueue between threads
Two threads reading the same immutable array
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: A pipe has a bounded kernel buffer, so the writer blocks when it is full. ArrayBlockingQueue is a textbook bounded buffer. A function call or shared read-only data has no buffer and no coordination.

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: Swapping the order of unlock(mutex) and signal(full) at the end of the producer cannot cause a deadlock.
options: True
False
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: Release order does not create a wait cycle. Signalling first just lets a consumer wake up and briefly wait on the mutex. Deadlock comes from acquire order, such as taking the mutex before wait(empty).

os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.prompt: A condition variable remembers a signal sent while no thread was waiting, so the next wait returns immediately.
options: True
False
os:producer-consumer-bounded-buffer.explanation: Condition variables are stateless; unmatched signals are lost. Semaphores do remember (the count goes up), which is why the CV pattern always pairs the wait with a predicate on shared state.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: Five dining philosophers each pick up the left fork, then the right. Making one philosopher pick up the right fork first removes deadlock. Which Coffman condition does that break?
options: Mutual exclusion
Hold and wait
No preemption
Circular wait
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: With one philosopher reversed, the forks are no longer all acquired in a ring, so no cycle can form. Philosophers still hold one fork while waiting for the other, so hold and wait remains.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: 12 tape drives total. P0 holds 5 (max 10), P1 holds 2 (max 4), P2 holds 2 (max 9), so 3 are free. Which Banker's safe sequence exists?
options: None; the state is unsafe
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: P1 needs 2 ≤ 3 and finishes, so 5 are free. P0 needs 5 ≤ 5 and finishes, so 10 are free. P2 needs 7 ≤ 10. P0 first fails because it needs 5 with only 3 free.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: Same system: 12 drives, P0 holds 5 (max 10), P1 holds 2 (max 4), P2 holds 2 (max 9). If P2 is granted one more drive, what is the resulting state?
options: Deadlocked
Safe, because 2 drives are still free
Unsafe, though not necessarily deadlocked
Safe, because P1 can still finish
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: With 2 free: P1 finishes, giving 4 free, but P0 needs 5 and P2 needs 6, so no full sequence exists and the state is unsafe. Unsafe means deadlock is possible if everyone asks for their maximum, not that it has happened. The Banker's algorithm refuses this grant.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: Two threads each lock their first mutex, fail tryLock on the second, release, and retry in lockstep. Neither makes progress, yet both use CPU. What is this, and what is the usual fix?
options: Deadlock; add a global lock order
Starvation; give one thread higher priority
Livelock; add randomised exponential backoff before retrying
Priority inversion; use priority inheritance
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: The threads are active, not blocked, but stay in sync, which is livelock. Random jitter breaks the symmetry. A global lock order removes the need for retries altogether, but the question describes the tryLock pattern.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: A function acquires every lock it needs at once before starting, and holds none while waiting. Which Coffman condition does that break?
options: Hold and wait
Circular wait
Mutual exclusion
No preemption
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: Hold and wait means holding some resources while requesting more. Getting all of them at once, or none, removes it, at the cost of holding locks longer than needed.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: In PostgreSQL, what does the deadlock_timeout setting control?
options: The maximum time a transaction may run
How long a backend waits on a lock before running deadlock detection
How long to wait before aborting any blocked query
How often autovacuum checks for lock conflicts
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: Detection is relatively costly, so Postgres waits deadlock_timeout (1 s by default) before checking for a cycle. The query-cancelling timeouts are lock_timeout and statement_timeout.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: Your app gets SQLSTATE 40P01 (deadlock_detected) from PostgreSQL. What should it do?
options: Retry the single failed statement inside the same transaction
Roll back and retry the whole transaction, with backoff
Ignore it; Postgres already retried for you
Raise lock_timeout so it never happens again
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: Postgres aborted your transaction as the victim, so the transaction is in a failed state and must be rolled back and retried from the start. Retrying one statement fails because the transaction is aborted.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: Two PostgreSQL transactions update account rows 1 and 2, one in order (1, 2) and the other in order (2, 1), and they deadlock occasionally. What is the best fix?
options: Use SERIALIZABLE isolation
Touch rows in a consistent order, such as SELECT ... ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE
Add an index on the id column
Lower deadlock_timeout to 10 ms
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: Locking rows in the same order breaks circular wait. SERIALIZABLE adds serialization failures rather than removing row-lock cycles, and a lower deadlock_timeout only detects the deadlock sooner.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: A Node.js service uses an async mutex library. Request A awaits lock X then lock Y, and request B awaits Y then X. Can this deadlock in single-threaded Node?
options: No; one thread cannot deadlock
No; the event loop detects cycles and rejects one promise
Yes; both requests await forever while the event loop keeps serving others
Yes; and the whole process freezes with 100% CPU
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: Deadlock is about a wait cycle, not threads. Each await yields, so the other request takes its first lock, and both promises then wait forever. The loop stays responsive, so it shows up as hung requests and timeouts, not a frozen process.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: A detector keeps a wait-for graph with single-instance resources. What does it run to find deadlocks?
options: Cycle detection, for example DFS, in O(V + E)
Dijkstra's shortest path
A topological sort that must include every lock
The Banker's safety check on every request
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: With single instances, a cycle in the wait-for graph means deadlock, and DFS finds one in linear time. The Banker's check is avoidance, run before each grant, not detection.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: When aborting a transaction to break a deadlock, which victim is generally preferred?
options: The oldest transaction, since it has waited longest
The one that is cheapest to roll back, while avoiding picking the same one every time
Always the transaction that requested the lock first
A random transaction outside the cycle
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: Rolling back the least work keeps waste low, and age or retry counts prevent the same victim starving. Aborting the oldest throws away the most work; aborting outside the cycle breaks nothing.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: Which situations can deadlock? Select all that apply.
options: A thread re-acquires a non-reentrant mutex it already holds
Two threads hold a shared read lock at the same time
Two threads lock A and B in opposite orders
Pool tasks block on subtasks queued to the same full pool
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: Self-deadlock, opposite lock orders and a pool waiting on itself all form a wait cycle. Shared read locks are compatible with each other, so concurrent readers never block each other.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: Which statements about deadlock prevention, avoidance and detection are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Prevention makes at least one Coffman condition impossible by design
Avoidance needs no advance information about what processes will request
Avoidance grants a request only if the resulting state is safe
Detection lets deadlocks happen, then recovers by aborting or preempting
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: Prevention removes a condition, avoidance checks safety before each grant, and detection cleans up afterwards. Avoidance (Banker's) needs each process's maximum demand in advance, which is its main practical weakness.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: A Java service backed by PostgreSQL has hung. Which tools help confirm a deadlock? Select all that apply.
options: A jstack thread dump
pg_locks joined with pg_stat_activity
Raising UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE
Doubling the JVM heap
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: jstack reports 'Found one Java-level deadlock' with the threads and monitors involved, and pg_locks plus pg_stat_activity show which backend waits on which. The other two are configuration changes, not diagnostics.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: All four Coffman conditions must hold for a deadlock, so breaking any one of them prevents it.
options: True
False
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: Mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and circular wait are jointly necessary. Each prevention technique, such as lock ordering or acquire-all, targets one of them.

os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.prompt: With multi-instance resources, a cycle in the resource-allocation graph is necessary but not sufficient for deadlock.
options: True
False
os:deadlock-detect-prevent-recover.explanation: Another instance may be freed by a process outside the cycle, which breaks the wait. With single-instance resources, a cycle is both necessary and sufficient.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: A Node LRU is a Map where get() deletes and re-sets a key. Which key does it evict when full?
options: The last key returned by map.keys()
map.keys().next().value, the first key in insertion order
The key with the smallest value
A random key
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: A Map iterates in insertion order, and delete-then-set moves a key to the end, so the first key is the least recently used. That gives O(1) LRU without writing a linked list.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: A cache holds 10 million entries: 32-byte keys, 200-byte values, and about 64 bytes of hash plus list-node overhead each. Roughly how much memory is that?
options: About 300 MB
About 3 GB
About 30 GB
About 30 MB
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: (32 + 200 + 64) bytes ≈ 296 bytes per entry, × 10^7 ≈ 2.96 GB. 300 MB is the result of dropping a zero. Real per-entry overhead in managed runtimes is often higher still.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: What is a common choice for the number of shards in a sharded LRU cache?
options: Exactly one per CPU core, never more
A power of two a few times the core count, indexed by hash & (n - 1)
One shard per key
A prime number much larger than the entry count
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: Several shards per core makes collisions between concurrent threads rare, and a power of two allows cheap masking (with a well-mixed hash). Too many shards waste capacity through imbalance.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: To coalesce concurrent misses, the cache stores an in-flight promise per key, and later callers await it. What must happen when the load fails?
options: Keep the rejected promise so future callers get the same error fast
Remove the in-flight entry so later callers can retry
Retry the load forever inside the cache
Evict the whole shard
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: Leaving a rejected promise cached turns one transient failure into a permanent error for that key. Remove it, or negative-cache it with a short, deliberate TTL.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: In Redis 7, what does raising maxmemory-samples from 5 to 10 do?
options: Makes eviction exact LRU
Brings eviction closer to true LRU at the cost of more CPU per eviction
Doubles the memory limit
Switches the policy to LFU
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: Redis samples candidate keys and evicts the best one from a small pool. More samples approximate true LRU better but cost more CPU. It never maintains an exact LRU list.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: Redis is used purely as a cache, and many keys have no TTL. Which maxmemory-policy fits?
options: noeviction
volatile-lru
allkeys-lru
volatile-ttl
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: allkeys-lru (or allkeys-lfu) can evict any key. volatile-* policies only consider keys with a TTL, so keys without one are never evicted. noeviction, the default, makes writes fail at the limit.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: A nightly job reads every key once, and afterwards hit rates crash for an hour. What is the problem, and what is a good fix?
options: False sharing; pad the shard locks
Scan pollution flushed the hot set; use an admission policy such as W-TinyLFU or segmented LRU
Lock contention; switch to a read-write lock
TTL expiry; raise the TTLs
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: Plain LRU admits every one-time key and evicts real hot keys. Frequency-aware admission or a probation segment keeps one-hit wonders out. Locking does not affect hit rate.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: A profile shows per-shard hit counters, stored next to each other in an array, bouncing between cores. What is the standard fix?
options: Make the counters volatile
Pad or align each counter to its own cache line
Use one global counter
Lower the number of shards to one
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: Neighbouring counters share a 64-byte line, so writes from different cores invalidate each other. Padding separates them; Java offers @Contended. volatile adds ordering but keeps the sharing.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: Why does an LRU cache use a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked one?
options: To store values twice for redundancy
So a node can be unlinked in O(1) given only a pointer to it
Because singly linked lists cannot be sorted
To make iteration from head to tail faster
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: The map gives a direct pointer to the node, and the prev pointer lets you splice it out without scanning. With a singly linked list, finding the predecessor is O(n).

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: Does an in-memory Map-based LRU in a Node process need locks?
options: Yes; every Map access needs a mutex
Not for synchronous get and put, but concurrent async loads for one key still need coalescing
No, and concurrent async loads are safe too
Only when running on more than one CPU core
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: JavaScript runs one call stack per isolate, so synchronous Map operations cannot interleave. Async loads can: two requests miss, both await the DB, and both write. Use promise-based singleflight for that.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: An LRU's put() adds a new node without checking if the key exists. What breaks when an existing key is updated?
options: Nothing; the map overwrites the old value
A stale node stays in the list, the size count drifts, and evicting it can delete the live entry
The hash function returns different buckets
get() becomes O(n)
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: The map now points to the new node, but the old one remains linked. When it reaches the tail, eviction deletes the key from the map and removes the live value. put must update in place and move the node to the head.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: Which designs keep a concurrent LRU cache correct? Select all that apply.
options: One mutex around both the map and the list
A ConcurrentHashMap for lookup with an unguarded shared linked list
Shards, each with its own lock, map and list
Lock-free reads that record accesses in a buffer drained under the lock
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: Each correct design guards the map and the list together, either with one lock, per shard, or by funnelling list updates through a locked drain. A thread-safe map does not make the linked list safe.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: Which statements comparing LFU and LRU are correct? Select all that apply.
options: LFU keeps frequently used items through a one-time scan
Naive LFU adapts slowly when popularity shifts because old counts linger
LRU needs a frequency counter per entry
TinyLFU uses a compact, aging frequency sketch to decide admission
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: Frequency resists scans but needs aging so stale popularity fades. TinyLFU's sketch makes that cheap. LRU tracks only recency (list position), not counts.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: Which pairs of operations must happen atomically, under the same lock, in a coarse-locked LRU? Select all that apply.
options: Lookup in the map and moving the node to the head
Computing the hash of the key
Inserting into the map and linking the node into the list
Unlinking the tail node and deleting its key from the map
Writing a log line for a cache miss
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: Each pair updates both structures, and a thread seeing them half-updated would see a corrupted cache. Hashing is a pure function of the key, and logging touches no shared cache state.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: A sharded LRU cache with N shards always evicts the globally least-recently-used entry.
options: True
False
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: Each shard evicts its own tail, so a busy shard may evict a fairly recent key while another shard holds much older ones. Sharding trades exact global LRU for concurrency.

os:thread-safe-lru-cache.prompt: In Node, a Map-based LRU used only from synchronous code on the main thread cannot have data races between get and put.
options: True
False
os:thread-safe-lru-cache.explanation: Only one piece of JavaScript runs at a time on the isolate, and synchronous code is never interrupted, so get and put cannot interleave. Races appear only across awaits or between worker threads sharing memory.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: A 32-bit address space uses 4 KiB pages and 4-byte page table entries. How large is a flat, single-level page table per process?
options: 4 KiB
4 MiB
1 MiB
4 GiB
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: 12 offset bits leave 20 bits of VPN, so 2^20 entries × 4 B = 4 MiB per process, mostly for unused space. 1 MiB is the entry count mistaken for bytes. This is why multi-level tables exist.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: x86-64 4-level paging translates 48-bit virtual addresses with 4 KiB pages. How are the bits split?
options: Four 9-bit table indices plus a 12-bit offset
Two 18-bit indices plus a 12-bit offset
Four 12-bit indices
Three 12-bit indices plus a 12-bit offset
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: 9 + 9 + 9 + 9 + 12 = 48. Each level is a 4 KiB page of 512 eight-byte entries, so 9 bits per index. 5-level paging adds another 9 bits for 57-bit addresses.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: With 4 KiB pages, VPN 0x402 maps to frame 0x1F. What physical address does virtual address 0x00402ABC translate to?
options: 0x0001FABC
0x001F2ABC
0x1F402ABC
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: Offset = low 12 bits = 0xABC, VPN = 0x402. Replace the VPN with frame 0x1F: 0x1F << 12 | 0xABC = 0x1FABC. Options that keep the 0x402 bits forgot to replace the page number.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: Reference string 7, 0, 1, 2, 0, 3, 0, 4 with 3 frames, starting empty. How many page faults do LRU and FIFO incur?
options: LRU 6, FIFO 7
LRU 7, FIFO 6
Both 6
LRU 5, FIFO 7
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: LRU misses on 7, 0, 1, 2, 3 (evicting 1) and 4 (evicting 2), hitting 0 twice: 6 faults. FIFO evicts 0 when 3 arrives, so the next 0 also faults: 7 faults. LRU keeps the recently used 0.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: A TLB has 1,536 entries. What is its reach with 4 KiB pages and with 2 MiB pages?
options: 6 MiB and 3 GiB
1.5 MiB and 1.5 GiB
6 MiB and 6 GiB
4 MiB and 2 GiB
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: Reach = entries × page size: 1536 × 4 KiB = 6 MiB, 1536 × 2 MiB = 3 GiB. That 512× gain is why databases and JVMs with large heaps use huge pages.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: Why does Redis log a warning at startup when Transparent Huge Pages are enabled?
options: THP disables the page cache
Copy-on-write after fork() copies 2 MiB pages, adding latency and memory during persistence
THP limits Redis to 2 GiB of memory
THP stops Redis from using swap
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: BGSAVE and AOF rewrite fork the process, and any write then copies a whole 2 MiB page instead of 4 KiB, inflating memory and latency. Background compaction can add stalls too.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: A process touches a page whose data is already in the page cache but not mapped in its page table. What kind of fault is this?
options: A major fault requiring disk I/O
A minor fault: the kernel just maps the existing frame
A segmentation fault
A TLB shootdown
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: Minor faults fix up the mapping without I/O; major faults must read from disk or swap. Shared libraries already loaded by other processes usually cause minor faults.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: After fork(), what happens when the child first writes to a page it shares with its parent?
options: The write goes straight to the shared page, and the parent sees it
A copy-on-write fault gives the child a private copy of that page
The entire address space is copied at that moment
The child is killed because the page is read-only
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: fork marks shared pages read-only and copies each page only when it is written. That keeps fork + exec cheap, and it is why a write-heavy parent can balloon memory during a Redis BGSAVE.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: A production host is thrashing: high major-fault rate, CPU mostly idle in iowait. What is the right first response?
options: Add more processes to soak up idle CPU
Reduce memory demand: lower concurrency, stop or move workloads, or tighten their limits
Lower the page size to 1 KiB
Disable the TLB
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: Working sets exceed RAM, so pages are evicted and immediately needed again. Shrinking total demand (or adding RAM) is the only fix. Adding processes is the classic mistake that makes thrashing worse.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: x86-64 long mode mostly disables segmentation. What do the remaining segment registers commonly provide?
options: Per-process page table roots
Thread-local storage through the FS and GS base registers
Memory protection for the stack
Separate code and data address spaces
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: CS, DS, ES and SS bases are treated as 0, but FS and GS bases still work. Linux uses FS for user-space TLS and GS for per-CPU kernel data. Page tables come from CR3, not segments.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: The Clock algorithm's hand reaches a frame whose reference bit is 1. What happens?
options: The frame is evicted immediately
The bit is cleared and the hand moves on, giving the page a second chance
The page is written back to disk and kept
The hand reverses direction
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: Clock evicts the first frame it finds with reference bit 0, clearing set bits as it passes. A page referenced again before the hand returns survives, which approximates LRU cheaply.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: On x86-64, where the hardware walks page tables, which statements about a TLB miss are correct? Select all that apply.
options: The MMU walks the page table without OS involvement
If the entry is present, the TLB is filled and the access continues
The kernel always runs to handle every TLB miss
If the entry is not present, a page-fault exception transfers control to the OS
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: x86 walks page tables in hardware, so most misses cost only extra memory accesses. The OS runs only on a page fault. Some architectures use software-managed TLBs, but x86-64 does not.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: Which statements about the dirty bit and page eviction are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Hardware sets the dirty bit when the page is written
A dirty page must be written back before its frame is reused
Evicting a dirty page costs nothing because stores go straight to disk
Replacement algorithms often prefer evicting clean pages
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: A clean page can be dropped and re-read later; a dirty one needs a write first, so enhanced Clock prefers clean, unreferenced pages. Stores go to RAM, not disk, so dirty eviction has a real I/O cost.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: Which are genuine benefits of paged virtual memory? Select all that apply.
options: Processes can use more virtual memory than physical RAM through demand paging
Every memory access becomes as fast as a cache hit
One physical copy of a shared library can be mapped into many processes
It removes the need for a TLB
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: Demand paging and page sharing are core benefits. Translation adds cost, which is why the TLB exists in the first place, and it makes nothing as fast as a cache hit.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: With 4 KiB pages, the low 12 bits of a virtual address pass through translation unchanged.
options: True
False
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: 2^12 = 4096, so the low 12 bits are the offset within the page, copied directly into the physical address. Only the page number is translated.

os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.prompt: Larger pages always reduce wasted memory because they need fewer page table entries.
options: True
False
os:paging-vs-segmentation-page-replaceme.explanation: They shrink page tables and TLB misses, but internal fragmentation grows: on average, half of the last page of each region is wasted, and that is 1 MiB with 2 MiB pages.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Cylinders 0-199, head at 53. Queue: 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. What is the total head movement under SSTF?
options: 640 cylinders
236 cylinders
208 cylinders
299 cylinders
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: SSTF order is 65, 67, 37, 14, 98, 122, 124, 183, and the moves add up to 12 + 2 + 30 + 23 + 84 + 24 + 2 + 59 = 236. 640 is FCFS in arrival order.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Same disk: cylinders 0-199, head at 53 moving toward higher cylinders, queue 98, 183, 37, 122, 14, 124, 65, 67. What is the total head movement under LOOK?
options: 331 cylinders
236 cylinders
299 cylinders
382 cylinders
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: LOOK goes up only as far as the last request: 53 to 183 is 130, then it reverses to 14, which is 169, for 299 total. 331 is SCAN, which travels to cylinder 199 before reversing.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: A 7,200 RPM HDD has an 8 ms average seek. Roughly how many random 4 KiB reads per second can it do?
options: About 80
About 800
About 8,000
About 7,200
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Average rotational latency is half a turn: 60 / 7200 / 2 ≈ 4.2 ms. Each random I/O costs about 8 + 4.2 ≈ 12 ms, giving about 80 IOPS. NVMe SSDs reach hundreds of thousands, which is why seek scheduling matters far less there.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: What is the average rotational latency of a 7,200 RPM disk?
options: About 8.3 ms
About 4.2 ms
About 1 ms
About 0.5 ms
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: One revolution takes 60 s / 7200 ≈ 8.33 ms, and on average the sector is half a turn away, so about 4.17 ms. 8.3 ms is a full revolution.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: On Linux, write() to a regular file returned successfully. Is the data durable if the machine loses power now?
options: Yes; write() only returns after the disk confirms
Not necessarily; it may still be in the page cache until fsync or fdatasync
Yes, as long as the file was opened read-write
Only if the file is smaller than 4 KiB
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Buffered writes land in the page cache and are flushed later. Databases call fsync (or use O_DSYNC/O_DIRECT) at commit for durability. Without that, power loss can drop acknowledged writes.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: epoll is a reactor-style readiness API. Which describes Windows IOCP and Linux io_uring?
options: Also reactors; they report when an fd is readable
Proactors; you submit the operation and are told when it has completed
Signal-driven I/O based on SIGIO
Blocking I/O with a thread per request
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: With readiness APIs you are told an fd is ready and then do the read yourself. With completion APIs you hand over the buffer and receive the finished result. libuv uses IOCP on Windows and epoll/kqueue elsewhere.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: On a busy Linux server, `free` shows little 'free' memory but plenty of 'available'. Why?
options: A memory leak is hiding the free memory
Most memory is page cache, which the kernel can reclaim when needed
Swap is counted as free
The kernel reserves memory for epoll
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Linux uses idle RAM to cache file data. 'available' estimates what can be reclaimed without swapping. Low 'free' on its own is normal, not a leak.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Several threads call epoll_wait on the same epoll fd. Which flag ensures a single ready socket is handled by only one thread at a time?
options: EPOLLET
EPOLLONESHOT
EPOLLIN
EPOLLRDHUP
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: EPOLLONESHOT disables the fd after one event is delivered; the handler re-arms it with epoll_ctl when done. EPOLLET alone can still wake another thread if more data arrives mid-handling. EPOLLEXCLUSIVE targets thundering herds across separate epoll instances.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: A server built on select() starts failing when a new connection gets file descriptor 1024. Why?
options: The kernel caps processes at 1024 sockets
fd_set is a fixed bitmap of FD_SETSIZE (usually 1024) bits
TCP has only 1024 ports below the ephemeral range
epoll is required once more than 1024 events are pending
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: select indexes a fixed-size bitmap by fd number, so fds at or above FD_SETSIZE overflow it. poll and epoll avoid this. The per-process fd limit (ulimit -n) is separate and adjustable.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Inside an fs.readFile callback, code calls setTimeout(a, 0) and then setImmediate(b). Which runs first in Node?
options: a, because timers are checked first
b, because the check phase follows the poll phase
It is nondeterministic
Both run in the same tick in source order
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: I/O callbacks run in the poll phase, and the check phase (setImmediate) comes next, before the loop returns to timers. At top level, outside any I/O callback, the order is nondeterministic.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: How does io_uring cut syscall overhead compared with read/write plus epoll?
options: It runs the application inside the kernel
Shared submission and completion rings let one syscall, or none with SQPOLL, cover many operations
It disables the page cache
It turns all files into sockets
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Applications push many submission entries and reap completions from shared-memory rings, batching work into one io_uring_enter. With SQPOLL a kernel thread polls the ring, so no syscall is needed. epoll still needs a syscall per read or write.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Which practices keep an event-loop server, such as Node, responsive? Select all that apply.
options: Keep CPU-heavy synchronous work off the loop
Use fs.readFileSync in request handlers for simplicity
Offload heavy computation to worker threads
Buffer partial reads and writes instead of assuming whole messages
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Any synchronous work stalls every connection, so keep the loop for I/O and move CPU work to workers. Sockets deliver arbitrary chunks, so you must frame messages. Sync fs calls in handlers block everyone.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Which statements about HDD scheduling algorithms are correct? Select all that apply.
options: FCFS minimises total head movement
C-SCAN gives more uniform waiting times than SCAN
LOOK reverses at the last pending request rather than at the disk edge
Deadline-style schedulers add per-request expiry times to bound starvation
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: C-SCAN serves in one direction then jumps back, evening out waits. LOOK skips empty travel. Deadlines fix SSTF/SCAN-style starvation. FCFS ignores position entirely and usually moves the most.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Which statements about the Linux page cache are correct? Select all that apply.
options: Recently read file data can be served from RAM without disk I/O
Writes are buffered and flushed later unless you use fsync or O_SYNC
Page cache memory can never be reclaimed by applications
O_DIRECT bypasses the page cache for that file's I/O
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: The cache speeds up reads and absorbs writes, and O_DIRECT opts out (some databases manage their own buffers). Clean cache pages are reclaimed whenever applications need memory.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: A read on a non-blocking socket with no data available returns immediately with EAGAIN/EWOULDBLOCK instead of waiting.
options: True
False
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: Non-blocking mode never sleeps in read; the caller learns 'not now' and waits for readiness through epoll. That is the building block of event loops.

os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.prompt: Edge-triggered epoll keeps reporting a socket as readable on every epoll_wait while unread data remains in its buffer.
options: True
False
os:disk-scheduling-and-io-models.explanation: That describes level-triggered mode. Edge-triggered reports only on a transition, when new data arrives, so you must read until EAGAIN or the remaining data can sit unnoticed.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Which Linux namespace gives a container its own process ID 1?
options: The mount namespace
The PID namespace
The UTS namespace
The user namespace
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: A PID namespace has its own numbering, so the first process inside is PID 1. UTS isolates the hostname, and mount isolates the filesystem view.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: `node server.js` runs as PID 1 in a container with no SIGTERM handler. `docker stop` waits 10 s and then kills it. Why?
options: SIGTERM is blocked by the seccomp profile
The kernel does not apply the default action for signals to PID 1 unless it installs a handler
Node ignores all signals inside containers
docker stop sends SIGHUP, not SIGTERM
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: PID 1 is special: unhandled SIGTERM is ignored, so Docker escalates to SIGKILL after the timeout. Add a handler, or use an init such as tini (docker run --init), which also reaps zombies.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: A host has 64 GiB RAM. Each VM needs 512 MiB of guest OS overhead plus 256 MiB for the app; each container needs only the 256 MiB app. Roughly how many more containers fit than VMs?
options: About the same
About 1.5x
About 3x
About 10x
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: VMs: 65,536 / 768 ≈ 85. Containers: 65,536 / 256 = 256. That is about 3x, because containers share one kernel instead of booting a guest OS each.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: In cgroup v2, what is the difference between memory.high and memory.max?
options: They are aliases
memory.high throttles and reclaims aggressively; reaching memory.max triggers the OOM killer
memory.max throttles; memory.high kills
memory.high applies to swap only
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: memory.high is a soft limit: the group is slowed down and pushed to reclaim. memory.max is the hard limit, where reclaim fails and the OOM killer runs inside the cgroup.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: A Node service runs in a container with a 512 MiB memory limit. What is the safest heap configuration?
options: --max-old-space-size=512 so the heap uses the whole limit
--max-old-space-size of about 350-400 MiB, leaving headroom for buffers, native memory and stacks
No flag; V8 always sizes from the host's total RAM correctly
--max-old-space-size=2048 to avoid GC pauses
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: The heap is not the only memory: Buffers, native addons, code and thread stacks live outside it. Setting the heap equal to the cgroup limit gets the container OOM-killed before V8 reports heap exhaustion.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: How does AWS Firecracker boot microVMs in about 125 ms while still using hardware virtualization?
options: It shares the host kernel like a container
A minimal KVM-based VMM with only a few virtio devices and no BIOS or PCI emulation
It snapshots the host process
It interprets guest code in user space
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Firecracker drops most legacy devices and firmware, emulating just virtio net and block, a serial console and little else, so the guest kernel boots almost immediately. Each microVM still has its own kernel behind KVM.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Where does Linux KVM fit in the type 1 / type 2 hypervisor split?
options: A pure type 2 hypervisor running as a normal app
A kernel module that makes Linux act as a type 1 hypervisor, usually paired with QEMU for devices
A container runtime
A paravirtual device driver for guests
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: KVM exposes CPU virtualization (VT-x/AMD-V) from the host kernel, so Linux itself is the hypervisor; QEMU or Firecracker provide the virtual devices. VirtualBox on a desktop is the usual type 2 example.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: A process in a container edits /etc/nginx/nginx.conf, a file that ships in the image. What happens with overlayfs?
options: The image layer is changed for every container
The file is copied up into the container's writable layer and changed there
The write fails because image layers are read-only
The change is written to the host's /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Image layers are shared and read-only. The first write copies the whole file up into the container's own writable (upper) layer and the edit lands there, so the image and other containers are unaffected, and the change is lost when the container is removed. Files Docker bind-mounts in, such as /etc/hosts and /etc/resolv.conf, are not in the image and skip copy-up.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: In a Node Dockerfile, why copy package.json and package-lock.json and run npm ci before copying the rest of the source?
options: npm ci requires an empty directory
The dependency layer stays cached and only rebuilds when the lockfile changes
It makes the final image smaller
It is required for multi-stage builds
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Docker reuses a layer until its inputs change. Copying the source first would invalidate the npm ci layer on every code edit. Multi-stage builds are what shrink the image.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Why is running a container with --privileged, or mounting /var/run/docker.sock into it, dangerous?
options: It only slows the container down
Either can give processes in the container root-level control of the host
It disables networking
It prevents the container from being stopped
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: --privileged grants all capabilities and device access; the Docker socket lets you start a new privileged container that mounts the host filesystem. Both are effectively host root.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: What is the purpose of Docker's default seccomp profile?
options: To encrypt container traffic
To block risky syscalls and shrink the kernel attack surface
To limit CPU usage
To isolate the hostname
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: seccomp filters syscalls, blocking things like kexec_load and mount by default. All containers share the host kernel, so every syscall they cannot make is one less exploit path. CPU limits are cgroups' job.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Which are shared by all containers on one Linux host? Select all that apply.
options: The host kernel
Each container's root filesystem view
The kernel's CPU scheduler
The PID numbers seen inside each container
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Containers are processes on one kernel and one scheduler. Mount namespaces give each its own root filesystem view, and PID namespaces give each its own numbering.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: You must run untrusted user code from the internet. Which approaches provide meaningful isolation? Select all that apply.
options: gVisor (runsc), which intercepts syscalls in a user-space kernel
Firecracker or Kata microVMs, each with its own kernel
Dropping all capabilities and applying seccomp as defence in depth
Running as root in a standard container with a read-only root filesystem
Putting it in its own network namespace and nothing more
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Shrinking or replacing the shared-kernel surface is what matters, plus layered hardening. A read-only filesystem or a separate network namespace alone leaves root with the full syscall surface of the host kernel.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: Which resources can cgroups limit? Select all that apply.
options: CPU time
The hostname visible to the container
Memory
Block I/O bandwidth
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: cgroups account for and limit resources such as CPU, memory, I/O and PIDs. Hostname isolation comes from the UTS namespace; namespaces control what a process sees, cgroups how much it uses.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: A Linux container can natively run an OS with a different kernel, because each container ships its own kernel.
options: True
False
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: Containers share the host kernel; images bring only user-space files. Running a different kernel needs a VM, which is how Docker Desktop runs Linux containers on macOS.

os:containers-vs-vms.prompt: To reach the host, a guest-kernel exploit in a VM usually also has to escape the hypervisor, whose interface is far smaller than the Linux syscall surface.
options: True
False
os:containers-vs-vms.explanation: The guest kernel is the attacker's own; the boundary is the narrow VM-exit and virtual device interface. That smaller surface is why VMs and microVMs are the standard for hostile multi-tenant code.
